titel: Long-term care and health insurance in old age
kurz: What Medicare covers and what it does not, why two retirees with the same savings can pay different premiums, what long-term care costs and when Medicaid steps in and looks at gifts made in the past five years.

bloecke.md:
At 65, almost everyone in the US becomes eligible for Medicare, the federal health insurance for older people. It covers hospital stays, doctors and prescription drugs, but with deductibles, coinsurance and premiums, and it does not cover long-term custodial care, that is, help with everyday activities over months or years. According to the federal Administration for Community Living, someone turning 65 today has almost a 70% chance of needing some type of long-term care services and supports in their remaining years.

Two things follow from this for your own planning. Health care in retirement has fixed costs that rise faster than general prices, and the largest risk, long-term care, has to be financed largely outside Medicare. The standard premium for Medicare Part B shows the trend: it has almost doubled since 2015.

bloecke.titel: Standard monthly premium for Medicare Part B, 2015-2026
bloecke.unter: The premium rose from $104.90 to $202.90 in eleven years, by 93%; it is deducted directly from the Social Security payment.

bloecke.md:
## Medicare in four parts

Medicare consists of four parts with their own rules. Part A, the hospital insurance, is premium-free for anyone who has worked and paid Medicare taxes for at least 40 quarters, that is, about ten years; spouses can qualify through each other. Part B covers doctors and outpatient care and has a monthly premium. Part C, Medicare Advantage, is a private plan that replaces A and B. Part D covers prescription drugs through private plans.

bloecke.md:
The initial enrollment period lasts seven months: the three months before the month you turn 65, that month and the three months after. Anyone who signs up for Part B later without having coverage from current employment pays a late enrollment penalty of 10% of the premium for every full 12 months of delay, for life. For Part D, the penalty is 1% of the national base premium for every month without equivalent drug coverage, also for life. People who are still working and are covered by an employer plan based on current employment can delay Part B without penalty and have eight months after that coverage ends to sign up. COBRA and retiree health coverage do not count as coverage from current employment.

Anyone with a health savings account must stop contributing once enrolled in any part of Medicare. If Part A is claimed after 65, it is granted retroactively for up to six months, though not before the month you turn 65, so contributions should end six months before enrollment.

## Medigap or Medicare Advantage

The most important decision at 65 is between two routes. Original Medicare (A and B) leaves 20% coinsurance without a cap. Most people therefore add a Medicare supplement policy (Medigap) and a separate Part D plan. Medigap policies are standardized by letter; since 2020, plans C and F are no longer available to people newly eligible, and Plan G is the most comprehensive option for them. The alternative is a Medicare Advantage plan, a private plan with a network, an annual out-of-pocket limit and often low premiums.

bloecke.md: The Medigap open enrollment period lasts six months, starting in the month in which you are 65 or older and enrolled in Part B. During this period, insurers must sell you any Medigap policy they offer at the standard price, regardless of your health. Afterwards, in most states, they may refuse you or charge more. A few states, such as New York and Connecticut, grant more extensive rights. Choosing Medicare Advantage at 65 and wanting to return to Medigap at 75 with a chronic illness can therefore fail.

## Premiums depend on income

Two retirees with the same coverage can pay very different premiums. Above certain incomes, Medicare charges an income-related monthly adjustment amount (IRMAA) on the Part B and Part D premiums. The basis is the modified adjusted gross income (adjusted gross income plus tax-exempt interest) from the tax return two years earlier; for 2026, this is the 2024 return. In 2026, the surcharge starts above $109,000 for single filers and $218,000 for married couples filing jointly and rises in five tiers; in the highest tier, the Part B premium is $689.90 a month instead of $202.90. The thresholds work as cliffs: a single dollar above a threshold triggers the full surcharge of that tier. What counts is the type of income, not the amount of assets.

bloecke.titel: Cost of a one-off income spike
bloecke.md:
A single retiree aged 66 normally has a modified adjusted gross income of $80,000. In 2026, she converts $100,000 from her traditional IRA to a Roth IRA in one go.

- Her income for 2026 is $180,000. In 2028, Medicare looks at this year.
- At the 2026 amounts, her Part B premium would be $527.50 instead of $202.90, that is, $324.60 more a month or $3,895 a year, plus a surcharge on Part D.
- If she spreads the conversion over four years at $25,000 each, her income stays at $105,000 a year, below the threshold of $109,000, and no surcharge applies.

The surcharge only applies for the year in question. If income falls because of a life-changing event such as retirement, the death of a spouse or divorce, the Social Security Administration can be asked on Form SSA-44 to use a more recent year.

## What long-term care costs and who pays

Medicare pays for care in a skilled nursing facility only after a hospital stay of at least three days as an inpatient, only for skilled care such as rehabilitation, and for at most 100 days per benefit period. Days 1 to 20 cost nothing; for days 21 to 100, a daily coinsurance applies, $217 in 2026. Custodial care, the help with bathing, dressing, eating or moving around that most people in need of care require, is not covered, neither in a facility nor at home.

Recent national cost surveys put the median cost of a nursing home at roughly $9,000 to $11,000 a month, depending on whether the room is shared or private, and costs differ widely by state. Assisted living and home care cost less, but they too are mostly paid privately. Medicaid, the means-tested program run by the states, is the largest payer of long-term care, but only once income and assets have largely been used up.

bloecke.titel: Four years in a nursing home (illustrative calculation)
bloecke.md:
The assumption is a cost of $10,000 a month, roughly the national median of recent surveys and considerably more in expensive regions.

- 48 months × $10,000 = $480,000
- Social Security of $2,400 a month after the Part B premium covers $115,200 of this.
- The remaining $364,800 has to come from assets, from insurance or, once these are used up, from Medicaid.

Unlike the costs of illness, these costs are not capped by any out-of-pocket maximum.

bloecke.titel: Cumulative funding gap with Social Security of $2,400 (illustrative calculation)
bloecke.unter: At an assumed $10,000 a month, the gap grows by $91,200 every year; there is no supplement that reduces it with the length of stay.

bloecke.md: With the move into a nursing home, rent or home costs, utilities and spending on food largely fall away. Part of the nursing home bill therefore replaces expenses that were incurred anyway before. A calculation that does not offset the previous household costs considerably overestimates the capital requirement, at least for a single person. For a couple, the costs of the home in which the other spouse continues to live remain. Most people who need care are looked after at home, mostly by family members. There the financial gap is smaller, but the caregivers often reduce paid work and lose earnings and, with them, future Social Security credits. This loss does not appear in any cost survey and falls mainly on women.

## Long-term care insurance

A traditional long-term care insurance policy pays an agreed daily or monthly amount once you can no longer perform two of six activities of daily living without help, or suffer from severe cognitive impairment, usually after a waiting period (elimination period) of 90 days, for example. Its disadvantage is the premium. It is not guaranteed; insurers have raised premiums on older policies considerably with the approval of state regulators. If the policy lapses at 80 because the premium can no longer be paid, most of what was paid in is lost.

Hybrid policies combine life insurance or an annuity with a long-term care benefit. Their premiums are often fixed, and if no care is needed, a death benefit remains; in return, they tie up a lot of capital. In states with a partnership program, partnership policies protect assets from Medicaid's spend-down rules dollar for dollar in the amount of the benefits paid. For tax-qualified policies, premiums can be deducted as medical expenses up to age-based limits if you itemize, and benefits are generally tax-free. A benefit that is not indexed loses purchasing power: at 2% inflation, $6,000 a month that becomes payable in 25 years has the purchasing power of only around $3,660.

bloecke.md:
## Medicaid and the look-back period

Medicaid is a joint program of the federal government and the states, and each state sets its own income and asset limits within federal rules. For nursing home care, the asset limit for a single person is $2,000 in many states. The home is usually exempt as long as a spouse lives in it or the person in care intends to return, up to an equity limit. For married couples, spousal impoverishment rules protect the spouse who stays at home: they keep a share of the joint assets and a minimum monthly income. After death, states must seek to recover the costs of long-term care for recipients aged 55 or older from their estate, which often means from the house (42 U.S.C. § 1396p(b)).

Adult children are generally not liable for their parents' care costs under federal law. Some states, however, have filial responsibility laws that allow a nursing home or the state to claim against children in certain cases. They are rarely enforced, but in 2012 a Pennsylvania court held a son liable for his mother's nursing home bill under such a law.

When someone applies for Medicaid for nursing home care, the state reviews all transfers of assets for less than their fair value in the 60 months before the application (42 U.S.C. § 1396p(c)). For gifts within this period, Medicaid imposes a penalty period during which it does not pay for nursing home care. It equals the amount given away divided by the average monthly cost of private nursing home care in the state: with a gift of $100,000 and a divisor of $10,000, Medicaid does not pay for ten months, and the clock only starts once the person would otherwise be eligible. Transfers to a spouse and to a disabled child are exempt, and the home can be transferred under certain conditions, for example to a child who has provided care for at least two years. Transferring the house to the children or to an irrevocable trust therefore needs time and careful planning, and it can conflict with the step-up in basis and with your own security.

bloecke.titel: Powers of attorney and health care directives
bloecke.md: Without a durable power of attorney for finances, nobody can manage your accounts, sell your house or deal with your IRA if you can no longer do so yourself. Spouses have no automatic authority over accounts in the other's name. A court then has to appoint a guardian or conservator, which takes time, costs money and is public. Three documents belong together: a durable financial power of attorney, a health care power of attorney or proxy with an advance directive, and a HIPAA authorization so that doctors may give information to the people you choose. The rules differ by state; many states have adopted the Uniform Power of Attorney Act, which obliges third parties to accept a valid power of attorney in most cases. Banks and brokers nevertheless often ask for their own forms, so it is worth checking with them in advance. Assets in a revocable living trust can be managed by a successor trustee without a court.

At the end of a withdrawal plan, the long-term care risk is a liquidity risk and not a return risk. It involves a need of the order of magnitude of the illustrative calculation above, several hundred thousand dollars over a few years, which arises in an unknown year. It can be covered by a policy whose premium is still affordable at 85, by a block of assets that remains unallocated to the very end, by home equity, or, once everything else is used up, by Medicaid. A withdrawal plan designed down to the last dollar for regular needs does not cover this need.

begriffe.text: Standardized private supplement insurance to Original Medicare that covers deductibles and coinsurance, depending on the plan letter. During the six-month open enrollment period from 65, it must be sold without a health check.

Private plan under Medicare Part C that replaces Parts A and B and usually includes drug coverage. It works with networks and prior authorization and has an annual out-of-pocket maximum for in-network services.

Surcharge on the Medicare Part B and Part D premiums for beneficiaries whose modified adjusted gross income from two years earlier exceeds certain thresholds. It rises in tiers, and a single dollar above a threshold triggers the full surcharge.

Six basic activities used to determine the need for long-term care: bathing, dressing, eating, toileting, continence and transferring, for example from bed to chair. Long-term care insurance usually pays if two of them cannot be performed without help.
